scope: Static reverse engineering of three externally flagged binaries; samples were not executed natively. Verdicts concern supplied artifacts, not their possible deployment by an attacker.

evidence: Parsed all CLR MethodDef bodies with dnfile/dncil. Main calls Run; Run binds HttpListener only to 127.0.0.1 and localhost on configurable port 47800.
Run reads/generates its own 32-byte device.key using ProtectedData CurrentUser and the RNG. No access to browser/OS credential stores was found.

LoadFiles hashes app.pak, compares its expected SHA-256, GZip-decompresses it, and reads uint16 filename-length / UTF-8 name / int32 content-length records. Extracted index.html (616829 bytes), player.html (5019), vendor/peerjs.min.js (92865). These are served as browser assets, not loaded as assemblies.

Handle rejects unexpected Host and cross-site writes. POST /device-key requires X-Atoms: 1; /save validates its Pictures/Documents root, rejects traversal/device names, normalizes the path, and writes under the application subdirectory. /quit and /bye manage the local instance.

EndOtherCopies queries WMI for its own executable basename and compares its port before killing stale copies. OpenBrowser launches the loopback URL with UseShellExecute=true. RegisterProtocol registers atoms: under HKCU Software/Classes; MakeDesktopShortcut uses WScript.Shell/CreateShortcut. No automatic-login trigger was found.

Decoded 10979 static decoder calls in index.html and 83 in player.html using only extracted decoder/rotation/wrapper functions in QuickJS. JavaScript implements encrypted IndexedDB storage, ECDH/AES-GCM messaging, PeerJS connections, explicit media-call controls, backup export, and user-selected sandboxed plugins. The player constrains video identifiers and verifies postMessage origins.

Fetched atomsconnections.com website, version.json, current portable ZIP, plugin catalog and its sole math plugin. Product purpose matches code. Plugin archive hash matches catalog 26bf4ce88d8d4834bdcf7e21867557109f8c9b5c95e93fd132a612366f941289; content is an arithmetic game with no network or host-execution primitive.

Bundled PeerJS exactly equals https://unpkg.com/peerjs@1.5.4/dist/peerjs.min.js (SHA-256 ad5d8870d1e389914f9cba8d35be313c4327c69ee0a221e482e9bf7621136fe5). Its WebRTC/STUN/TURN functions support the stated peer messaging purpose.
samples.external_label_explanation: Unsigned small .NET application with a large high-entropy compressed/obfuscated web resource, DPAPI, process management and protocol registration plausibly attracted ML/PUA detections. These observations do not establish hostile behavior.

evidence: Traced ELF entry 0x40e5f3 into C runtime startup and main 0x40d280; main initializes its process arguments, handles special CLI modes and constructs/executes the application object.
Fetched upstream v6.26.0 Linux-static release archive; SHA-256 fc6f8ae5f64e4f17481f7e3be29a1c56949f216a998414188003eae1db20c9e5 matches published release checksum.

Official xmrig length is 8350992 bytes, SHA-256 b20f39fc00d242e706b6c30367ad811c676e0575050a4ec2f30104b696944b49. All 8350992 bytes match the beginning of the 8351056-byte sample. Its only difference is a 64-byte opaque suffix after the ELF section table; no changed ELF header, code, configuration, or initializer redirects execution into it.

Upstream executable implements Stratum job authorization/subscription/submission and CPU/GPU proof-of-work, normal pool/config CLI options, optional daemonization and HTTP API. Kernel MSR/hugepage facilities optimize mining. Reviewed upstream App.cpp, BaseConfig.cpp and RxMsr.cpp and release config. No bot command surface, exploit, worm, credential theft, persistence installer or imposed attacker wallet was added.
samples.external_label_explanation: XMRig is frequently used for unauthorized mining, and the collector basename systemd-ntpd suggests such deployment. This file contains upstream miner code; the basename, reputation and opaque trailer alone do not prove cryptojacking or Mirai behavior.

evidence: PE entry at 0x4013cc passes the VB5! project structure to ThunRTMain. Recovered the VB6 form event at 0x4026e0, ReadServerEXE at 0x4024e0, name-matching process search at 0x402f80, and termination helper at 0x402d50 with rizin and Capstone.

ReadServerEXE opens its supplied executable path, gets file length, subtracts 99 (one-based VB file position) and reads a fixed 100-byte string using __vbaGetFxStr4. It splits the record on tilde and retains the first item as target path.

The form constructs its own App.Path/App.EXEName plus .exe and invokes ReadServerEXE. It takes the final component of the resulting target path, puts it into List1, passes that value into the process search, then calls rtcKillFiles on the full target path and ends. It uses On Error Resume Next.

Resolved VB6 DllFunctionCall descriptors rather than guessing from adjacent strings: 0x401d7c OpenProcess; 0x401dc0 CloseHandle; 0x401e0c TerminateProcess; 0x401e80 GetWindowThreadProcessId; 0x401ee4 AdjustTokenPrivileges; 0x401f30 OpenProcessToken; 0x401f80 LookupPrivilegeValueA; 0x401fcc GetCurrentProcess; 0x402014 Process32First; 0x402048 Process32Next; 0x40209c CreateToolhelp32Snapshot.

Search walks PROCESSENTRY32 records, case-folds executable names and selects a matching PID. The helper enables SeDebugPrivilege, requests PROCESS_TERMINATE with OpenProcess, calls TerminateProcess and closes the handle. These are removal capabilities, not evidence of password theft.

The final 100 bytes of this supplied file are all zero; it contains no configured target path. No credential store, input capture, network transport, persistence or payload execution path was recovered. The only DLL dependencies are standard VB6/Windows runtime facilities.
samples.external_label_explanation: This resembles a builder-generated removal component, and the project path mentions a server/new builder. Such a helper may have circulated with malware or matched generic VB6 signatures. Neither that provenance nor kill/delete APIs establishes a hostile target; this copy is unconfigured.

trait_changes: Moved Activator type-name evidence to metaprogramming/reflection with exact consumers updated. It is object construction/reflection, not staged-code execution.

Moved KillProcess helper-name evidence to metadata/binary/symbols/name. Preserved the name matcher and the MSBuild composite consumer; the name neither establishes .NET identity nor proves process termination.

Restored TerminateProcess name-reference coverage for Microsoft Visual/native artifacts while retaining system-language runtime catalog suppression. Added exact OpenProcess binary-name coverage with unused Go runtime names excluded, and a structured VB6 fixed-string file-read import trait.
Raised neutral CUDA/OpenCL references to notable. No cryptojacking inference was introduced.

At the two full destination directories, eliminated the worker-name transparent OR grouping by inlining its three alternatives in its sole consumer (unchanged AND/OR semantics), and consolidated the redundant Python imported-module getattr query onto the existing first-argument provenance matcher. The latter also rejects an import in the name argument and accepts a tracked module alias.
